definitions.definition: A homeless ascetic outside the Vedic sacrificial order; the rival teachers of DN 2 and the Buddha and Mahāvīra are all śramaṇas; Aśoka pairs 'brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas' as the two orders found everywhere.
A samaṇa is one who has calmed (samita) evils, lives in calm (samacariyā) and harms no one.
One is a samaṇa not by shaving the head but by equanimity (samayā).

notes: Śramaṇa is paired with brāhmaṇa as perpetual enemies in the Mahābhāṣya (on P 2.4.12).

definitions.definition: Leaving the household for the homeless life; its first visible fruit is the honour paid even to a slave who has gone forth.
Title given in the Pali canon to each of the six famous teachers as founder of a religious 'ford'.
(Jain) tīrthaṅkara: a Jina who founds the fourfold community; Gosāla claimed to be the last of this age (as reported in Bhagavatī 15).
Epithet of the six teachers: 'having an order, a following, teacher of a following' (saṅghī gaṇī gaṇācariyo).
The visible fruit of the ascetic life, the question Ajātasattu put to all six teachers and to the Buddha.
A hall where ascetics, brahmins and wanderers of various sects met to debate; the six teachers' claims about their dead disciples were discussed there.
(Ājīvika, as reported) The end that fool and wise alike reach after the fixed round of 8,400,000 great aeons.
(Early Buddhist) The end reached by cutting off craving, not by transmigration.
Pali name for the Jain ascetics and for their teacher Nātaputta; DN 2 reports his doctrine as the fourfold restraint.

literal: one who lives (by a rule of) livelihood

definitions.definition: A member of the naked ascetic order of Gosāla and his predecessors; the name appears in the Pali and Jain canons, the Arthaśāstra, Aśoka's edicts and inscriptions, and Tamil works.

notes: The etymology 'one who follows his profession / keeps the livelihood rule' is debated; Buddhist texts pun on ājīva (livelihood).

definitions.definition: (As reported) The destiny that, with circumstance (saṅgati) and nature (bhāva), transforms all beings, who have no control, power or energy; all things are fixed (niyayā savvabhāvā).
One of five co-operating causes (with time, own-nature, former deeds and effort): wrong view when held alone, right view when held with the others.
(As reported) The second of the three shaping forces (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva); the Jain Sūtrakṛtāṅga calls the fixed experience of beings 'saṅgaiya'.

notes: Meaning disputed by translators (circumstance, environment, class-association).

definitions.definition: (As reported) The third shaping force: each being's own nature (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā).
(As reported) The Ājīvika doctrine that beings are purified simply by passing through the whole fixed round of births.
A doctrine of 'some ascetics and brahmins' rejected by the Buddha: purity does not come through transmigration.
(As reported) The simile of the fixed round: as a ball of string thrown runs out unwinding to its end, so beings run through saṃsāra to the end of suffering.

(As reported) One of six classes — black, blue, red, yellow, white, supremely white — through which beings pass; the supremely white are the three Ājīvika leaders (AN 6.57, ascribed to Pūraṇa); in the Tamil report, black, dark blue, green, red, golden, white, with release in the supremely white birth.
The Buddha's six: dark or bright birth yielding a dark result, a bright result, or nibbāna.

equivalents.note: the Jain six colour-classes of soul (leśyā) are also six and colour-named; the texts draw no link

definitions.definition: (As reported) The Ājīvika measure of the fixed round: 8,400,000 great aeons through which every being passes.
(As reported) One of the eight 'stages of a person' in Makkhali's lists; Buddhaghosa glosses them as stages of life from the newborn onward.
(Jain report) Gosāla's doctrine, drawn from the regrowing sesame plant, that beings may die and re-enter a body; he claimed to be the seventh such re-entry.
(Jain report) A destructive fiery power gained by severe austerity; Gosāla learnt its method from Mahāvīra and used it to burn two monks and against Mahāvīra.
A supernormal fiery power (labdhi) of ascetics; Mahāvīra's cool power (śītaleśyā) counters it.
The cooling power by which Mahāvīra saved Gosāla from Vesiyāyaṇa's fiery power.
(Jain report) The eightfold prognostication Gosāla learned from the six disācaras, drawn from the Pūrvas.
The eightfold lore (year-lore, dreams, marks, portents, bodily signs, omens and the rest) by which some claim to know the future; the Jain text says it sometimes fails and gives no release.
(Jain report) Six wandering teachers who drew the Mahānimitta from the Pūrvas and taught Gosāla.
(Jain report) The 'eight finalities' proclaimed around Gosāla's death: last drink, song, dance, salutation, storm-cloud, sprinkling elephant, battle of stones, and the last tīrthaṅkara.
(Jain report) Four kinds of drink permitted and four not permitted, taught by the dying Gosāla.

notes: Items not recalled reliably; not listed.

definitions.definition: (Tamil report) The Ājīvaka's lord: 'the boundless knower' present in all things everywhere and always.
(Tamil report) Four kinds of beginningless, indestructible atoms — earth, water, fire, air — which with life (uyir) make the five principles.
In the Isibhāsiyāiṃ's chapter of Maṅkhaliputta, the steadfast one who is not moved and does not turn into this or that state, and so saves himself and others from saṃsāra.
(As reported) Pūraṇa's doctrine that the doer does no evil and the giver gains no merit.
One of the four 'assemblies' of disputants: those who deny action; 84 kinds; they hold the world barren and fixed.

notes: The Pali and Jain uses overlap but are not identical: the Jain class is wider (it includes denial of the categories of soul etc.).

literal: doctrine of action / of the efficacy of deeds

definitions.definition: The doctrine that deeds are effective, taught by all Buddhas (kammavāda, kiriyavāda, viriyavāda); the one Ājīvaka who went to heaven held it.
The first 'assembly': 180 kinds; the true kiriyavāda is taught by one who knows self and world, influx, stopping and wearing away of karma; a rival 'kiriyāvāda' of intention alone is rejected.
(As reported) That beings are defiled and purified without cause or condition; ascribed to Makkhali (DN 2) and to Pūraṇa (SN 22.60, SN 46.56).
One of the three sectarian tenets that end in inaction.
(As reported) The view that there is no gift, no fruit of deeds, no this world or other world, no spontaneously born beings.
The same view as held by Pāyāsi, answered by Kumāra Kassapa.

equivalents.note: the natthika denial of the other world entails annihilation at death (DN 2 joins them in Ajita's speech)

definitions.definition: (As reported) Ajita's doctrine that fool and wise alike are annihilated at the breaking of the body.
One of the extremes: seven grounds for asserting the annihilation of an existing being, from the four-element self to the self of the highest formless sphere.

literal: made of the four great elements

definitions.definition: (As reported) 'This person is made of the four great elements', which at death return to their masses.
Beings reborn without parents (gods, hell-beings); Ajita and Pāyāsi deny them; Sañjaya refuses to declare on them.
(As reported) There is no other world, because there is no one who goes to it.
One of the four topics on which Sañjaya refuses every alternative.
(As reported) Pakudha's seven unmade, barren, unmoving bodies: earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and soul.
(As reported) The same seven, called eternal and uncuttable, in the Ājīvika-like doctrine of Guṇa.
(As reported) Epithet of Pakudha's seven bodies and of the eternalist's self and world: barren, peak-steady, pillar-firm.
The akiriyavādins' world is 'barren and fixed' (vañjho niyao).
(As reported) The soul is the seventh of Pakudha's unmade bodies; the Ājīvika texts (as reported) speak of 'all souls' (sabbe jīvā) as powerless.
(As reported) For the materialist the soul is the body itself, bounded by the skin (tajjīva-taccharīra).
(Buddhist report) Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's teaching: the Nigaṇṭha is curbed, yoked, cleansed and pervaded by all 'waters' (vāri).
(Jain account) Cāujjāma, the law of four restraints taught by Pārśva, as against Mahāvīra's five vows.
(As reported) Evasion by refusing every alternative; the fourth ground (dullness) is Sañjaya's formula.
A wrong view arising from fear of false speech, of grasping or of cross-examination, or from dullness.

equivalents.note: the Pali eel-wrigglers and the Jain annāṇiyas both refuse to affirm; the Jain class (67 kinds) is wider

definitions.definition: King Ajātasattu's name for Sañjaya's answer.
The four forms — is, is not, both, neither — in which each of Sañjaya's four questions is put and each refused.

notes: The term catukkoṭi is later than DN 2; the fourfold question form is in the text.

definitions.definition: (Jain report) The fourth 'assembly': 67 kinds; its adherents hold ignorance better than knowledge — 'who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it?'.
The ignorant cannot settle their inquiry in ignorance or instruct others.
(Jain report) The 'assembly' of those who hold that discipline or reverence (vinaya) alone leads to the good: 32 kinds — veneration of eight objects by mind, speech, body and gifts.
The Jain frame in which all rival doctrines fall into four assemblies: kriyā, akriyā, ajñāna, vinaya — 363 kinds in all.
(Jain report) That five elements — earth, water, fire, air, space — exist and from them a self arises that perishes with them.

literal: the soul is that, the body is that

definitions.definition: (As reported) The soul is the same as the body: bounded by the skin, it ends when the body dies.
'The soul is the body' and 'the soul is one thing, the body another' are both extremes that make the holy life impossible.

equivalents.note: the same identification of self with body, named differently in Jain and Brahmanical reports

definitions.definition: (Jain report) That the one knower appears manifold throughout the world, as one earth-mound appears manifold.
(Jain report) That the self neither acts nor causes action.
(Jain report) Five elements and the self as sixth, all eternal.
(Jain report) Five kinds of denier — staff, rope, thief, partial and total — who cut off the doctrine of the soul, rebirth, compassion, or everything.

notes: Etymology uncertain (utkala / utkaṭa); the gloss 'one who cuts off' follows the chapter's own use of vocchedaṃ / chedaṃ vadati.

definitions.definition: Four grounds for holding self and world eternal, three from meditative recollection of past lives or aeons and one from reasoning.
Four grounds for holding some beings eternal and others not: Brahmā as creator, gods corrupted by play, gods corrupted by mind, and the reasoner's eternal mind.
Four grounds for holding the world finite, infinite, both, or neither.
Two grounds for holding self and world arisen without cause: recollection from the non-percipient gods, and reasoning.
Sixteen grounds for holding the self percipient after death.
Eight grounds for holding the self non-percipient after death.
Eight grounds for holding the self neither percipient nor non-percipient after death.
Five grounds for holding supreme nibbāna here and now: sense pleasure, or one of the four absorptions.
Gods who fall from their state through excessive play; one of the grounds of partial eternalism.
Gods without perception who fall when perception arises; one who recalls only that arising holds that self and world arose by chance.
A speculative view; the sixty-two grounds are views of those who do not know or see, conditioned by contact and craving.
The sixty-two grounds as a fine-meshed net in which every theorist is caught.
One who holds a view by reasoning and inquiry rather than meditative experience; a ground in several classes of the sixty-two, and the third unreliable teacher of MN 76.
Reasoners who follow their own speculation cannot escape suffering.
Quality of the truths the Tathāgata knows beyond all sixty-two views.
Every one of the sixty-two views is experienced through contact at the six sense-bases.
The 'safe bet' teaching: affirming another world and the fruit of deeds is the wiser course whether or not they exist.

literal: doctrine that all is due to past deeds

definitions.definition: One of the three sectarian tenets; ascribed to the Nigaṇṭhas in MN 101.
One of the three sectarian tenets: that all experience is due to God's creation.
The element of initiative (with persistence, exertion etc.) whose evident existence refutes the view that no one acts of his own doing.
(As reported) Denied by Makkhali: there is no doing by self or other, no human effort, strength or vigour.
(Prakrit purisakkāra-parakkama) Affirmed by Mahāvīra against Saddālaputta; one of the five co-causes.
Doing by oneself and by others exists, as the element of initiative shows.
(As reported) 'There is no exertion, action, strength, energy, human effort' — Gosāla's formula in the Jain canon.
Energy, whose efficacy all Buddhas teach against Makkhali's 'there is no energy'.

literal: doctrine that time is the cause

definitions.definition: Time as sole cause, one of the five one-sided causal views (with own-nature, destiny, former deeds, effort) that are wrong alone and right together.
(As reported) Pūraṇa denies it: giving, self-control and truthfulness bring no merit.
(As reported) Pūraṇa denies that the doer incurs it.
(As reported) The Ājīvikas' severe austerities; yet no austerity ripens unripe karma in their doctrine.
Patience is the highest austerity; a fool's fasting is not worth a sixteenth of understanding the Dhamma.
Austerity without right knowledge, 'not worth a sixteenth part' of well-taught dharma.
The mark by which one is a śramaṇa (Utt 25.32).
Wrong faith; that taught by others falls into the four vāda classes, or five kinds: one-sided, perverse, doubting, vainayika, ajñānika.

literal: extended in / directed to the world (of the people)

definitions.definition: The school's name: the view that only this world, as far as the senses reach, exists; the doxographies call it the teaching most people follow.
In the Arthaśāstra, one of the three branches of investigation (ānvīkṣikī), with Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

cross_language.note: Tibetan name of the Lokāyata/Cārvāka school
in the Pali canon a branch of brahmanical learning (disputation/nature-lore), not clearly the school

definitions.definition: Name of the materialist school, after its legendary teacher Cārvāka, Bṛhaspati's disciple; explained by Guṇaratna as those who 'chew up' merit, demerit and the unseen.
Name for the Lokāyatas as followers of Bṛhaspati; Kamalaśīla calls the deniers of inference 'Bārhaspatyas and others'.
A school of statecraft holding that only economics and government are sciences, the Veda being a cover.

notes: Whether the two uses name the same school is not settled by the texts.

definitions.definition: (Opponents' designation) The Cārvāka as 'crest-jewel of the nāstikas': one who denies the other world, the fruit of deeds and the Veda.
(As reported) Earth, water, fire and air — the only principles; space is not counted.
(As reported) The principles are the four elements; Jayarāśi: the sūtra states them only to reflect worldly belief, and not even they stand examination.
(As reported) Body, sense-organ and object are only names for aggregates of the elements.
(As reported) Consciousness is produced (or manifested) by the elements when transformed into a body and perishes with them.
(As reported) The simile for emergent consciousness: as the power to intoxicate arises from kiṇva and other ingredients, none of which has it alone.

literal: doctrine that the body is the self

definitions.definition: (As reported) The person is the body qualified by consciousness ('I am fat, I am thin').

notes: Sadānanda's Vedāntasāra (tea:vedantasara:refutation) distinguishes Cārvākas who take the gross body, the senses, the breath or the mind as self.

literal: perception (as the only means of knowledge)

definitions.definition: (As reported) Perception alone is a means of knowledge; Jayanta calls this the view of the uneducated Cārvākas, and Jayarāśi overturns even perception's definition.
(Lokāyata, reported variously) One (perception); or not fixable in number (suśikṣita); or none establishable (Jayarāśi).
(As reported) Not a means of knowledge, since pervasion cannot be established; or (Purandara) valid only as known in worldly life.
(As reported) Cannot be known by perception, inference, testimony or comparison; hence inference fails.
(As reported) A hidden extra condition that can never be ruled out, so no concomitance is certain.

literal: inference as known in the world

definitions.definition: (Purandara) The worldly inference the Cārvākas accept, as against inference that transgresses the worldly path to reach the unseen.
(As reported) The cause of the world's variety — fire hot, water cold — in place of any unseen cause.
One of five co-causes; wrong view if held alone.
(As reported) Denied: there is no unseen cause; the variety of things is from own-nature.
(As reported) Pleasure is the only human aim; the pain mixed with it is to be avoided as the fish's bones are.

notes: The Prabodhacandrodaya gives artha and kāma as the two aims.

definitions.definition: (As reported) Liberation is nothing but the destruction of the body; not knowledge.
(As reported) If the śrāddha fed the dead, oil on a quenched lamp would feed its flame; the rites for the dead are a brāhmaṇa livelihood.
(Jayanta's report) Refined Cārvākas who say the number of means of knowledge cannot be fixed, and who grant a knower lasting as long as the body but deny it beyond.
Jayarāśi's thesis that no principle can be established, since no means of knowledge can be defined.
Jayarāśi's description of everyday practices, which go on though no principle is established.
(As reported) For the Bārhaspatyas the Veda is a mere cover for one who knows the course of the world.
(As reported) The parable of faked wolf-tracks: as the tracks deceive, so the learned deceive with talk of unseen things; the world is only as much as the senses reach.
